caption: Figure 0.0.1: Like a builder laying the first bricks, this chapter establishes the essential foundations of machine learning, neural networks, and PyTorch that every subsequent chapter will build upon.
Figure 0.1.1: Gradient descent navigates a loss landscape by following the steepest downhill direction at each step, seeking the lowest valley (minimum loss).
Figure 0.1.2: Overfitting versus generalization: the model on the left has memorized every training point (including noise), while the model on the right captures the underlying pattern.
Figure 0.2.1: Neural networks are layered machines: raw inputs flow in, pass through layers of learned transformations, and emerge as predictions.

Figure 0.2.2: Backpropagation as an assembly line. The quality inspector (loss function) finds a defect and passes blame backwards through each worker (layer), who adjusts their tools (weights) proportionally to their contribution to the error.

Figure 0.2.3: Dropout as a classroom exercise. By randomly putting some neurons to sleep during each training step, the remaining neurons cannot rely on their neighbors and must learn robust, independent features.
Figure 0.3.1: The PyTorch workbench: tensors as raw materials, autograd as the differentiation engine, GPU acceleration, and the training loop that ties them together.

Figure 0.3.2: Tensors as building blocks. A scalar is one block, a vector is a row, a matrix is a flat grid, and a 3D tensor is a cube. PyTorch lets you stack, reshape, and slice these blocks at will.

Figure 0.3.3: The training loop as a racetrack. Each lap (epoch) passes through the same four stations: forward pass, loss computation, backward pass, and optimizer step. The robot gets a little better each lap.

Figure 0.4.1: Reinforcement learning is like training a dog. The dog (agent) tries different actions in the room (environment) and receives treats (rewards) only for the desired behavior, gradually learning which tricks earn the biggest reward.

Figure 0.4.2: PPO as careful cooking. Instead of dumping the entire salt shaker (unconstrained policy update), PPO clips each update to one small measured pinch at a time, preventing catastrophic over-correction.
Figure 1.1.1: A timeline of NLP breakthroughs. Each dot represents someone saying 'this changes everything' and, for once, being mostly right.
Figure 1.1.2: The four eras of NLP, each step building on the last. Rule-based systems gave way to statistics, which yielded to neural networks, which finally evolved into transformers.
Figure 1.1.3: The NLP task zoo: from classifying sentiment to translating languages, these are the problems that keep NLP researchers employed (and occasionally frustrated).

Figure 1.1.4: Why language is hard. A robot encounters ambiguity (the duck dilemma), coreference puzzles (which thing is too big?), and pragmatic traps (passing the salt when asked "Can you pass the salt?").
Figure 1.2.1: Bag-of-Words vs. word embeddings. Sparse representations treat every word as independent, while dense embeddings place semantically similar words near each other in vector space.
Figure 1.2.2: The filing cabinet analogy. Bag-of-Words stores one tally per word in a vast, mostly empty filing cabinet. Word embeddings compress meaning into a compact set of continuous dials.
Figure 1.3.1: The Skip-gram architecture. A center word is fed through an embedding layer, and the model learns to predict surrounding context words. The hidden layer weights become the word vectors.

Figure 1.3.2: Negative sampling. Instead of computing probabilities over the full vocabulary, the model only distinguishes the true context word from a handful of random negatives, reducing computation by orders of magnitude.

Figure 1.3.3: A 2D projection of word embedding space. Semantically related words form clusters, and meaningful directions emerge (e.g., the gender direction from "king" to "queen" parallels "man" to "woman").
Figure 1.4.1: The polysemy trap. Static embeddings assign one vector to "bank" regardless of context, producing a blurry average that captures none of its distinct meanings well.

Figure 1.4.2: The ELMo architecture. A forward and backward LSTM each process the full sentence, and the outputs from multiple layers are combined with learned weights to produce a contextual embedding for each token.

Figure 1.4.3: Word embeddings as a GPS for meaning. Just as GPS coordinates let you compute distances and directions between locations, embedding vectors let you compute semantic relationships between words.
Figure 2.0.1: Before a language model can read a single word, it must first slice text into pieces; tokenization is the invisible gatekeeper that decides where one "word" ends and the next begins.

Figure 2.1.1: Tokenization as sushi preparation. The chef (tokenizer) must slice the text roll into pieces that are small enough to fit the vocabulary but large enough to preserve meaning. Too many tiny pieces waste the context window; too few large pieces limit what the model can express.

Figure 2.1.2: Tokenization artifacts as a broken telephone game. When the tokenizer splits words at unexpected boundaries, the resulting fragments can confuse the model, leading to arithmetic errors, inconsistent spelling, and strange behavior at token boundaries.

Figure 2.2.1: BPE as a puzzle-piece factory. Workers scan the conveyor belt for the most frequently adjacent pair of blocks, glue them together into a new token, and repeat. The result is a vocabulary of mixed-size pieces optimized by frequency.

Figure 2.2.2: Two philosophies of vocabulary construction. BPE and WordPiece build from the bottom up by merging small pieces. Unigram works top-down, starting with a massive vocabulary and sculpting away the least useful pieces until the optimal set remains.
Figure 2.3.1: Special tokens are the traffic cops of your input sequence, telling the model where sentences start, stop, and what deserves extra attention.

Figure 3.0.1: From the forgetful telegraph operator of the RNN to the spotlight of attention, this chapter traces the breakthrough idea that lets a model learn where to look instead of compressing everything into a single vector.
Figure 3.1.1: An RNN processes tokens one at a time, like a telegraph operator transcribing a message word by word. By the time the message gets long, the earliest words have faded from memory.

Figure 3.1.2: The vanishing gradient problem visualized: like a goldfish whose memory fades with each passing moment, a vanilla RNN loses track of early tokens as the sequence grows. The information on those early "sticky notes" becomes unreadable.
Figure 3.2.1: Attention lets a model shine a spotlight on the most relevant parts of the input at each step, rather than relying on a single compressed summary of the entire sequence.

Figure 3.2.2: Attention as a detective board: strings of varying thickness connect source tokens to target tokens, forming a soft alignment. Thicker strings indicate stronger attention weights, revealing which source words the model focuses on for each output word.

Figure 3.3.1: Multi-head attention assigns multiple "detectives" to the same sequence. Each head learns to focus on a different type of relationship: one tracks syntax, another tracks coreference, a third tracks semantic similarity.
Figure 4.0.1: The Transformer, depicted as a layered machine of self-attention and feed-forward blocks, is the architectural blueprint behind every modern large language model.

Figure 4.1.1: The Transformer as a layer cake: embedding at the base, with alternating attention and feed-forward layers stacked on top. Each layer adds richness to the representation, and residual connections (the frosting) keep gradients flowing smoothly.
Figure 4.2.1: Building a Transformer from scratch: each component (attention heads, feed-forward layers, embeddings) is assembled step by step on the workbench, following the architectural blueprint.

Figure 4.3.1: The three Transformer families: encoder-only models (like BERT) read bidirectionally, decoder-only models (like GPT) generate left to right with causal attention, and encoder-decoder models (like T5) combine both approaches.

Figure 4.4.1: GPU memory as a city: the fastest SRAM is a small neighborhood at the center, surrounded by larger but slower HBM districts. Data must travel along bandwidth-limited highways between them, making memory access patterns critical for performance.

Figure 4.5.1: Transformers excel at certain computational tasks but struggle with others. Understanding their expressiveness limits explains why chain-of-thought prompting helps: it provides the intermediate steps that a fixed-depth network cannot compute internally.

Figure 5.0.1: A probability distribution alone does not produce text. Decoding strategies are the bridge between a trained model and the words it generates, each method trading off creativity, coherence, and speed.

Figure 5.1.1: Greedy decoding always takes the steepest uphill step, while beam search explores multiple paths in parallel. The greedy hiker may reach a local peak, but the beam searcher is more likely to find the true summit.

Figure 5.2.1: Temperature controls the entropy of the sampling distribution, like a DJ controls the energy of a mix. Low temperature produces focused, deterministic outputs; high temperature flattens the distribution, allowing rare tokens to surface more often.

Figure 5.3.1: Speculative decoding pairs a fast apprentice model with an expert verifier. The apprentice drafts multiple tokens quickly; the expert checks them in a single pass, accepting correct ones and rewriting the rest.

Figure 5.4.1: Autoregressive models paint one stroke at a time from left to right. Diffusion models start with a blurry canvas and refine the entire image simultaneously, trading sequential precision for parallel generation.
